newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British Steel pays price of firm pound.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British Steel pays price of firm pound.

text.p: British Steel Plc counted the cost of the pound's relentless rise in world currency markets on Monday as its annual profits collapsed and forced it to launch a new cost-cutting drive which will cull more jobs.

Pretax profits were more than halved to 451 million pounds ($736.8 million) from 1.1 billion the previous year. The annual dividend was frozen at 10 pence per share and turnover was up a mere two percent at 7.22 billion pounds.
British Steel's shares were down 5-3/4 pence at 157-1/2 pence after the results, although the sharp fall in profits had been anticipated.
Sir Brian Moffat, chairman and chief executive, admitted the year had been a "difficult" one, but made clear the pound's pain was not over despite brightening prospects in the steel market.
"The steel trading outlook for 1997/98 is one of cautious optimism, although concerns remain about the current strength of sterling and its serious impact on our future profits."
He issued a warning that the pain would be felt across Britain's export industry.

"The strength of sterling is a problem to British Steel and to many of its UK customers who are also significant exporters. Their order books are bound to be affected later this year if sterling remains at its present level," said Moffat.
As a result of the profit collapse, Moffat announced three price-cutting initiatives on Monday. The first is to speed up the job cutting programme.
British Steel did not detail job cuts or the potential cost in its latest results statement.
Recent press reports have indicated that the group could axe up to 10,000 jobs in five years, compared with the regular 500 to 1,000 jobs shed per annum.
A group spokesman told Reuters earlier this year the group would axe "significantly more than 5,000 jobs over five years" at a cost of tens of millions of pounds.
The other two cost cutting drives will be in raw materials, supplies and services and improving use of information technology.

The root of its woes is the pound which has risen more than 20 percent against the mark since last summer leaving companies like British Steel exposed. Much of the group's mainland European sales is denominated in marks.
Some 80 percent of its sales are sterling-sensitive and some 55 percent of sales are generated outside Britain.
As well as being hit by sterling strength in mainland European markets, the company has also suffered cheaper competitors scooping up business in Britain.
British Steel's results also faced a separate blow of weak steel prices last year, dealing a double whammy to its profitability.
The profit slump was in line with analysts' forecasts which ranged from 380 million to 575 million pounds after a spate of downgrades which began in late 1996.

Current trading conditions provided one bright spot in the results statement, however. Demand was described as "buoyant" in Britain, the U.S. and the Far East, with some improvement also seen in mainland Europe.
The group added that it was still looking for expansion opportunities in Asia and the Far East. Capital expenditure in the year stood at 413 million pounds. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
